articles.title: Scientists find a weak spot in one of the deadliest brain cancers
articles.summary: Researchers may have found a new way to weaken glioblastoma’s defenses against treatment. Blocking a protein called SET prevented tumors from forming in preclinical models, while targeting related proteins made cancer cells more vulnerable to radiation. The strategy works by restoring activity of PP2A, an enzyme that glioblastoma cells appear to suppress. Human testing will be needed to determine whether the approach is safe and effective.
articles.content:
Glioblastoma is among the most lethal forms of cancer, and treatment options have changed relatively little because the tumors frequently withstand both radiation and chemotherapy. Researchers at The Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center - Arthur G. James Cancer Hospital and Richard J. Solove Research Institute have now identified a protein called SET as a possible target that could make glioblastoma cells easier to kill with existing therapies.

Rather than replacing current treatments, the strategy is designed to help them work better. In preclinical experiments, suppressing SET prevented tumors from developing.

A Potential Weakness in Glioblastoma

Among the proteins examined, SET stood out because blocking it had such a strong effect on tumor formation. The researchers also found that interfering with related proteins increased the sensitivity of glioblastoma cells to radiation.

Together, the findings point to a biological pathway that may eventually be targeted with drugs to weaken the cancer's defenses.

The OSUCCC - James team focused on PP2A, an enzyme involved in regulating signals that cancer cells use to grow, survive, and recover from treatment-related damage. Glioblastoma cells appear to interfere with PP2A using three proteins called ANP32A, CIP2A and SET. When the researchers blocked those proteins in laboratory and animal models, fewer cancer cells survived, and the remaining cells became more vulnerable to radiation.

"Glioblastoma is hard to treat because it can adapt and survive," said Arnab Chakravarti, MD, chair of radiation oncology at the OSUCCC - James. "Our findings suggest that restoring PP2A activity may make glioblastoma cells less able to survive treatment. That gives us a clear path to test whether this approach can make radiation and chemotherapy more effective for patients with GBM."

Testing Ways to Restore PP2A Activity

The results remain preliminary and have not yet been evaluated in patients. Researchers are now investigating whether SET or other proteins that suppress PP2A can be targeted safely and whether doing so improves the effectiveness of standard glioblastoma therapies.

The team also examined an FDA-approved antipsychotic drug that is capable of increasing PP2A activity. According to the researchers, the results provide additional reason to study medications that influence this pathway.

However, the drug is not ready to be used as a glioblastoma treatment and should not be taken for this purpose outside a clinical trial.

"This is an important first step," said Chakravarti. "By understanding how SET and related PP2A blockers help GBM survive treatment, we can test ways to block that protection and make current therapies more effective."

A First Step Toward New Treatment Strategies

The study was published in the May 2026 issue of Cancer Letters, and was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute and The Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery identifying a protein target that could improve treatment effectiveness for glioblastoma, one of the deadliest brain cancers. This breakthrough has broad potential impact on patient outcomes and represents meaningful progress in cancer therapy research. The article provides detailed context about the mechanism, experimental results, and future clinical implications, making it a substantive and hopeful development in health science.

articles.title: Ada Yonath obituary: Crystallographer who overcame ‘impossible’ challenge of mapping the ribosome
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02801-0Nobel laureate persisted despite widespread derision and revolutionized structural biology by protecting fragile crystals.
articles.content:
Credit: Micheline Pelletier/Corbis/Getty

Grit and determination feature in most scientific careers, but the Israeli structural biologist Ada Yonath surmounted more obstacles than most. Yonath was the first to grow crystals suitable for X-ray analysis that would reveal the structure of the ribosome — a macromolecular complex that functions as a factory for proteins in living cells and is fundamental to implementing the genetic instructions to make a living organism. For this work, she won a share of the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Yonath was the fourth of eight women ever to win the chemistry Nobel, and the first since Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin, 45 years previously. But she never saw her gender as important, saying, “I am a scientist, not male or female. A scientist.”

Yonath, who has died aged 87, explored the interaction of antibiotics that were known to exert their effects through binding to bacterial ribosomes. These studies not only revealed how such compounds disrupt ribosomal function, but also shed light on antibiotic resistance and opened up the possibility of designing new drugs.

Making samples one billion times bigger lets simple microscopes pinpoint amino acids

Born Ada Lifshitz in Jerusalem to an impoverished Orthodox Jewish family, Yonath lost her father when she was 11 years old. Her parents had little education themselves, but they encouraged her insatiable curiosity. Despite having to take evening and weekend jobs to support her family, she graduated from Beit Hakerem (now Hebrew University Secondary School), an academically rigorous secular institution, and completed undergraduate and master’s degrees at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. She obtained a doctorate in structural biology at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Tel Aviv, Israel, working on the protein collagen.

After completing postdocs at the Mellon Institute (a forerunner of Carnegie Mellon University) in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania and at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, she returned to the Weizmann Institute in 1970 to set up Israel’s first biological crystallography laboratory. Although she initially studied individual proteins, she conceived the idea of working out the structure of the ribosome.

It was an impossible task with the technology available at the time, and she was widely ridiculed. The ribosome is composed of a large and a small subunit, which together comprise a complex of protein and ribosomal RNA amounting to some hundreds of thousands of atoms — more than ten times larger than any molecule solved previously.

How to win a Nobel prize: what kind of scientist scoops medals?

Furthermore, X-ray crystallography requires a crystal — and no one had so far crystallized the large, asymmetric and flexible ribosome. Yonath went to West Germany to work at the Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics in West Berlin, with its director Heinz-Günther Wittmann, whose lab was devoted to the study of ribosomes from many different species. With his support and contributions from his colleagues, Yonath was able to tackle a challenge that would take decades.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights Ada Yonath's groundbreaking scientific achievement in crystallography that revolutionized understanding of the ribosome, a fundamental biological structure. Her work has broad significance in health and medicine, particularly in antibiotic research and drug design, benefiting society at large. The article provides substantial context about her challenges, scientific impact, and legacy, making it an inspiring story of perseverance and scientific progress.

articles.title: Daily briefing: GLP-1 obesity drugs slow signs of ageing in mice
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02781-1Mice on GLP-1s also performed better on cognitive tasks than those on a calorie restricted diet . Plus, satellite images showed early warning signs of glacier collapse near the Nepal–Tibet border and the impact of people saying fewer words aloud.
articles.content:
Mice on GLP-1s also performed better on cognitive tasks than those on a calorie restricted diet . Plus, satellite images showed early warning signs of glacier collapse near the Nepal–Tibet border and the impact of people saying fewer words aloud.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

The flash flood destroyed many buildings and left villages covered in mud and debris.Credit: Arun Sankar/AFP via Getty

Satellite images taken just days before the high-altitude collapse of rock and ice that caused a catastrophic flash flood in Nepal showed concerning signs of an unstable glacier system, geophysicist Manoochehr Shirzaei tells Nature. However, such events are still difficult to predict using existing monitoring systems, he says. An effective early-warning system would need to integrate several approaches that screen glacial regions, ramp up surveillance of any that are identified as potentially unstable and model what might happen in the event of a collapse.

Nature | 5 min read

The GLP-1 medication semaglutide — sold as Wegovy for the treatment of obesity — might have anti-ageing properties, a study in mice suggests. Researchers found that older female mice taking a GLP-1 drug lived longer than did mice not taking one, and the treatment slowed several biological changes associated with ageing, such as inflammation. The treated mice also performed better at cognitive tests than did untreated mice on a strict diet, which suggests the drug has benefits that aren’t explained by calorie reduction alone, says biologist and study co-author Danica Chen.

Nature | 5 min read

Reference: Nature paper

130,000 The number of baby common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) that researchers have released into the Adriatic Sea this year. Their aim is to curb the booming population of blue crabs (Callinectes sapidus), which are muscling out other species in the Mediterranean. The octopuses will prey on the crabs — if they survive to adulthood. (Scientific American | 4 min read)

The Canadian government has announced that the nation’s universities have recruited 64 international researchers as part of a campaign to attract foreign talent. Forty-eight of these researchers are moving from the United States, taking up positions in fields ranging from health sciences to engineering. The group will receive a total of 500 million Canadian dollars (about US$360 million) in funding for eight years. Many US scientists face funding uncertainty as the administration of President Donald Trump attempts to cut research grants.

Nature | 5 min read

California blackworms (Lumbriculus variegatus) can move faster in confined spaces than they can in open ones. Researchers found that the tiny worms could zip through narrow tubes that were only around twice their width in around one minute, but took much longer to traverse wider channels — results that held true in computer models of strings of beads. The findings could inform the design of robots that squeeze through tight spaces, which could be used to slither through rubble or deliver drugs inside people’s bodies.

Science News | 4 min read

Reference: Physical Review Letters paper

Features & opinion

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope was launched to map the invisible Universe, but its biggest discoveries could emerge from its use beyond this goal, argues astronomer Priyamvada Natarajan. The telescope’s data will immediately become public, enabling scientists to interrogate its findings for their own research goals, and one quarter of the instrument’s operational time will be allocated to pursuits that can deviate from its core objectives. “Transformative scientific infrastructure does more than answer the queries that justified its construction. It expands the realm of questions that can be asked at all,” Natarajan writes.

Nature | 5 min read

In a world of self-service and remote working, people are speaking fewer words aloud each day now than they were 20 years ago, and the decline is particularly pronounced in people under the age of 25. This dwindling number of spoken words could have knock-on effects, some researchers worry. Replacing speech with text-based messages bypasses some of the cognitive effort required to listen and respond to another person, and saved message histories eliminate the need to remember what’s been said — shortcuts that could cause long-lasting changes in the brain over time.

The Washington Post | 8 min read (free registration required)

Reference: Perspectives on Psychological Science paper

Image of the week

This cookie, called a µBite, was made from recycled plastic and food waste. Researchers used a process called oxidative hydrothermal dissolution to break down polyethylene terephthalate and crop offcuts such as corn stalks into small molecules. They then fed these molecules to engineered yeast that can convert them into an edible, 3D-printable slurry. A stint in the microwave solidifies the printout into a biscuit. The team have yet to taste their creation, but say the treats smell good enough to eat. (Science Alert | 4 min read)

Reference: American Chemical Society meeting abstract (SIU Carbondale Communications)

articles.title: Compound in blueberries may help muscle cells burn excess fat
articles.summary: Scientists in Japan have identified a natural compound found in blueberries, grapes, and other berries that may help muscle cells burn excess fat instead of storing it. The compound, pterostilbene, reduced abnormal fat buildup in cultured mouse muscle cells by boosting fat breakdown and helping stabilize a key protein involved in fatty acid metabolism.
articles.content:
Excess fat stored inside skeletal muscle has become an important metabolic health concern. This type of fat buildup can be encouraged by high-fat diets, physical inactivity, and aging. Unlike fat stored under the skin, lipid droplets that accumulate within muscle cells can interfere with normal muscle function and make it harder for the body to efficiently use glucose and fatty acids. Over time, this reduced metabolic flexibility can contribute to insulin resistance. Finding ways to limit excess fat inside skeletal muscle could therefore be important for supporting healthy aging and reducing the risk of lifestyle-related disease.

One pathway that plays an important role in this process involves peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor δ (PPARδ). When PPARδ signaling is active, it promotes fatty acid oxidation and helps limit the accumulation of lipids inside cells. Researchers have become increasingly interested in food-derived bioactive compounds that may influence this pathway, but exactly how these substances affect PPARδ has remained unclear.

A Berry Compound Targets Muscle Fat Metabolism

A research team in Japan led by Associate Professor Takakazu Mitani of Shinshu University has now identified pterostilbene as a natural dietary compound that can stabilize PPARδ and influence fat metabolism inside muscle cells.

Pterostilbene is a naturally occurring polyphenol found in blueberries, grapes, and other berries. Previous research has linked the compound to beneficial metabolic effects in the liver and adipose tissue, but scientists knew much less about how it might affect skeletal muscle. The new findings were published in Volume 83 of the Food Bioscience journal on September 1, 2026.

"We currently lack approved treatments specifically targeting myosteatosis," says Dr. Mitani. "This critical gap led our team to screen food-derived compounds for natural, dietary interventions. During the screening, we identified pterostilbene and focused our investigation on uncovering its precise mechanism of action."

Screening Food Compounds for Fat Reduction

To investigate potential natural treatments, the researchers tested a collection of food-derived phytochemicals using cultured C2C12 mouse skeletal muscle cells. They examined whether the compounds could reduce abnormal fat accumulation inside the cells without interfering with normal muscle development.

Among the compounds tested, pterostilbene produced the strongest reduction in intracellular lipid accumulation. Importantly, the treated muscle cells continued to grow and differentiate normally.

Further experiments showed that pterostilbene did not work by preventing fatty acids from entering the muscle cells. Instead, the researchers detected increased release of glycerol outside the cells, which is an important sign that stored fat is being broken down.

The treated cells also showed greater expression of genes involved in fatty acid oxidation. Together, these results suggest that pterostilbene encourages muscle cells to break down stored lipids and process them for energy.

Protecting a Key Fat Metabolism Protein

The researchers then investigated the molecular mechanism behind these effects and found that pterostilbene significantly increased PPARδ signaling.

The way it accomplished this was unexpected. Many experimental compounds designed to stimulate PPARδ work by binding directly to the receptor and activating it. Pterostilbene appeared to operate differently.

Instead of directly activating PPARδ, the compound increased the amount of PPARδ protein present inside the cells. It did this by preventing the protein from being broken down through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.

By slowing the degradation of PPARδ, pterostilbene allowed more of the protein to remain available inside the cell. This stabilization increased PPARδ transcriptional activity and boosted the activity of genes involved in lipid metabolism.

"Our findings establish a scientific framework for developing functional foods and nutritional supplements that target muscle fat metabolism. However, beyond the potential of pterostilbene itself, this work provides an experimental framework for identifying other natural compounds that can stabilize the PPARδ protein," mentioned Dr. Mitani.

Potential Implications for Metabolic Health

With metabolic diseases becoming increasingly common worldwide, the findings provide a starting point for studying dietary approaches that could eventually contribute to strategies for obesity, type 2 diabetes, and age-related metabolic decline.

However, the results are still limited to molecular experiments in cultured mouse muscle cells. They do not yet demonstrate that pterostilbene can prevent or treat these conditions in animals or humans.

Even so, the researchers say the compound could serve as a promising candidate bio-ingredient for the food and healthcare industries as they explore new functional products aimed at muscle fat metabolism.

Additional in vivo research will be necessary to determine whether the effects translate beyond cultured cells. Future studies will also need to evaluate effectiveness, safety, and how selectively pterostilbene acts on its intended biological targets before the findings can be developed into practical nutritional or pharmaceutical applications.

articles.personality_title: Natural compound in berries helps muscle cells burn excess fat

This issue is linked to aging, poor diet, and lack of exercise and can lead to diseases like diabetes.

**What happened** – Researchers in Japan found that a natural compound called pterostilbene, which is found in blueberries, grapes, and other berries, helps muscle cells break down extra fat. They tested this on mouse muscle cells grown in the lab and saw that pterostilbene prevented fat from building up by protecting a protein called PPARδ that controls fat burning.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it shows a new way to help muscles use fat better. Pterostilbene works by stopping the breakdown of the PPARδ protein, allowing muscles to burn fat more efficiently. This could lead to new foods or supplements that help reduce the risk of metabolic diseases like obesity and type 2 diabetes.

**What's next step** – Scientists need to test pterostilbene in animals and people to see if it works safely and effectively outside the lab. They also want to find other natural compounds that act in similar ways. This research could eventually lead to new treatments or health products focused on muscle fat metabolism.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A natural compound in berries may help muscle cells burn excess fat by protecting a key protein, offering a new approach to support metabolic health.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un composé naturel des baies aide les muscles à brûler l’excès de graisse
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques étudient comment l’excès de graisse à l’intérieur des cellules musculaires peut causer des problèmes de santé. Contrairement à la graisse sous la peau, la graisse stockée dans les muscles gêne l’utilisation normale de l’énergie et est liée au vieillissement, à une mauvaise alimentation et au manque d’exercice.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs japonais ont découvert qu’un composé naturel appelé ptérostilbène, présent dans les myrtilles, les raisins et d’autres baies, aide les cellules musculaires à décomposer l’excès de graisse. Ils ont testé cela sur des cellules musculaires de souris en laboratoire et ont observé que le ptérostilbène empêche l’accumulation de graisse en protégeant une protéine nommée PPARδ, qui contrôle la combustion des graisses.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car elle montre une nouvelle façon d’aider les muscles à mieux utiliser les graisses. Le ptérostilbène agit en empêchant la dégradation de la protéine PPARδ, ce qui permet aux muscles de brûler la graisse plus efficacement. Cela pourrait conduire à de nouveaux aliments ou compléments pour réduire le risque de maladies métaboliques comme l’obésité et le diabète de type 2.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques doivent tester le ptérostilbène sur des animaux et des humains pour vérifier son efficacité et sa sécurité en dehors du laboratoire. Ils cherchent aussi d’autres composés naturels qui agissent de manière similaire. Cette recherche pourrait aboutir à de nouveaux traitements ou produits de santé ciblant le métabolisme des graisses dans les muscles.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Un composé naturel des baies pourrait aider les cellules musculaires à brûler l’excès de graisse en protégeant une protéine clé, ouvrant une nouvelle voie pour soutenir la santé métabolique.

Qué pasó** – Investigadores en Japón encontraron que un compuesto natural llamado pterostilbeno, presente en arándanos, uvas y otras bayas, ayuda a las células musculares a descomponer la grasa extra. Lo probaron en células musculares de ratón en el laboratorio y vieron que el pterostilbeno evita la acumulación de grasa al proteger una proteína llamada PPARδ que controla la quema de grasa.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo es importante porque muestra una nueva forma de ayudar a los músculos a usar mejor la grasa. El pterostilbeno funciona al evitar que se descomponga la proteína PPARδ, permitiendo que los músculos quemen grasa más eficientemente. Esto podría llevar a nuevos alimentos o suplementos para reducir el riesgo de enfermedades metabólicas como la obesidad y la diabetes tipo 2.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos deben probar el pterostilbeno en animales y personas para ver si funciona de manera segura y efectiva fuera del laboratorio. También quieren encontrar otros compuestos naturales que actúen de forma similar. Esta investigación podría llevar a nuevos tratamientos o productos de salud enfocados en el metabolismo de la grasa muscular.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Un compuesto natural en bayas puede ayudar a las células musculares a quemar grasa extra protegiendo una proteína clave, ofreciendo un nuevo enfoque para apoyar la salud metabólica.
